title: How to Automate Captions With Auto Caption Tools in 2026
summary: Built-in tools automate captions with just minor corrections needed.
body_markdown:
## Stage 3: Automate the hand-off with Activepieces


A new video lands in a folder, the captioning service gets called, and a reviewer is pinged with the SRT. Activepieces, which MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run in production, does the carrying for you. It doesn't write captions itself.


The Drive, HTTP and Slack steps all sit in one flow, with an Agent step placed in that same flow beside them, and the run trace for that flow is a single logged execution from the new file to the Slack message, not two systems bridged by a callback.


A missing SRT link points to the exact step that dropped it.


Because the text comes from the captioning tool, the errors you plan to review come from there too.


What Activepieces removes is the manual download, upload and "did anyone check this?" message that otherwise eats the afternoon you saved, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so the free plan's 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows cover a thousand runs a month.


The flow below shows the whole chain in six steps, so you understand how the steps connect. The thing to take from it is that review is built in as the last human-facing step, not left as a habit.


1. Google Drive, New File trigger on the watched folder.
2. HTTP call to the captioning service with the file.
3. Poll for the result until the job finishes.
4. Save the SRT back to the Drive folder.
5. Post to Slack with a link to the SRT.
6. Run the Test step.


In the editor, each stage maps to one block, and the next three subheadings take them in order.


### Trigger: new video in a watched folder


Pick the Google Drive integration and its New File trigger, then point it at one dedicated folder.


Keep that folder for videos only; a trigger watching a busy shared folder will fire on every stray document and spend your plan's credits on files that were never meant for captioning.


If your team uses Dropbox, the equivalent new-file trigger works the same way. Either way, the trigger hands the next step the file's name and ID, and those are the fields you map from here on.


### Action: send to the captioning service and wait for the result


Add an HTTP action that sends the video, or a link the service can read, to your captioning tool's API. Map the file name and link from the trigger into the request.


Captioning jobs rarely finish instantly, so follow the call with a polling step that checks the job status and continues only once the transcript is ready.


Check how your plan counts steps before you set the polling interval. A loop that checks every few seconds can burn through credits on a long video, and a slower interval costs you only a short wait.


### Action: save the file and notify a reviewer


Once the result arrives, add a Drive action that saves the SRT into the same folder as the video, named to match it. Then add a Slack message to the reviewers' channel with the file name and a link to the SRT.


Test the flow with a short clip before trusting it, using the Test step to confirm each mapped field carries real values. A blank link in a Slack message is the kind of silent failure that lets unreviewed captions go live.
